analysis.one_liner: Requires meatpackers to publicly disclose cattle contracts and buy a minimum share of cattle through open negotiation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction in March 2023 it was sent to the House Agriculture Committee's livestock subcommittee and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced large beef packers to file their standard cattle purchase contracts with the Agriculture Department, which would publish them in a public library so ranchers can see the real terms before signing [S2]. It also would have required the biggest packers — those slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle — to buy a set minimum share of cattle through open, negotiated markets rather than closed formula contracts, with fines up to $90,000 per violation for failing to comply [S2]. The aim is to give independent ranchers better price information and bargaining power against a few very large buyers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators gain the most. Under current practice, a handful of large packers buy most fed cattle through private formula contracts, so ranchers negotiate with little visibility into what terms other sellers are getting. The bill would give them a public catalog of contract types, premiums, and discounts [S2], require 14-day advance reporting of cattle scheduled for slaughter so sellers can time their sales [S3], and force the largest packers to keep buying a minimum share of cattle on open markets where prices are publicly discovered [S2]. Consumers could benefit indirectly if more competitive bidding disciplines beef prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent cattle ranchers and feedlot operators

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public cattle contract library: packers must file each type of contract they use — duration, premiums, discounts, and delivery commitments — and USDA must publish it in a monthly report available to all producers, so a rancher can see the terms of deals before negotiating one [S2].

Requires the largest packers (those slaughtering an average of 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle over five years) to purchase a mandatory minimum percentage of cattle through approved pricing mechanisms — negotiated purchases, negotiated grid purchases, stockyards, or open trading platforms — rather than locking everything into private formula contracts [S2].
Attaches real enforcement: up to $90,000 in civil penalties per violation, with each week of a continuing violation counted as a separate violation [S3].

Improves market information generally: 14-day advance reporting of slaughter schedules, expedited daily carcass weight reporting, and annual cutout yield reporting give sellers a clearer picture of demand and value [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large beef packing companies that would qualify as covered packers — those slaughtering at least 5% of the nation's fed cattle. They would bear the cost of filing detailed contract information with USDA, shifting a share of purchases from flexible formula contracts to negotiated markets, and potential fines of up to $90,000 per violation per week [S2, S3]. Indirectly, if negotiated bidding raises the prices packers pay for cattle, some of that cost could pass through to consumers in higher beef prices. USDA would also need funding to run the library and reporting systems [S3].

drawbacks.text: Forcing packers to buy a minimum share of cattle through negotiated markets reduces the flexibility of formula contracts that both packers and some large feeders use to manage volume and risk, and any added procurement costs could eventually show up in retail beef prices for consumers [S2].

The mandatory minimums are set by rulemaking, with a floor of the 2020–2021 average share of negotiated purchases in each region and a cap of 50%, so the actual requirements could land at modest levels and be revised every five years in consultation with industry representatives [S3].

The maximum penalty of $90,000 per violation (counted weekly) is small relative to the revenues of packers large enough to be covered, which could weaken the deterrence the enforcement system depends on [S3].

The reporting regime carries administrative costs: packers must file detailed contract data, and USDA must build and maintain the public library and new reports, with appropriations left open-ended [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent ranchers the upside is concrete: real visibility into contract terms and a guaranteed open-market share of purchases in regions where negotiated trade has thinned out. The costs fall on a handful of very large packers and, potentially, marginally on beef consumers, and the bill's own design softens them — minimums are region-specific, phased through rulemaking with cost-benefit analysis, and allow shortfalls to be remedied in later periods. The weak point is enforcement: a $90,000 weekly cap may not move companies this size. On balance the bill is a modest, targeted fix rather than a sweeping restructuring of the cattle market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2023, sent to the House Agriculture Committee's livestock subcommittee a month later, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Feenstra (R-IA) introduced the Cattle Price Discovery and Transparency Act of 2023 on March 1, 2023, with a Democratic and a Republican original cosponsor — Rep. Andy Levin (D-MI) and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA) [S1, S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced, and on April 4, 2023 it was referred again to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry [S5].

That was the last action of record. The subcommittee and full committee never held a markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest beef packing companies are better off: with no vote ever taken, they face no public contract library, no mandatory negotiated-purchase minimums, and no penalties, and they keep buying cattle under their existing private formula arrangements.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only recorded supporters were its Republican sponsor and two original cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican.

industries.note: The handful of packers slaughtering 5% or more of the nation's fed cattle would have had to file every contract type they use with USDA for public release, buy a minimum share of cattle on open negotiated markets instead of private formula contracts, and face fines up to $90,000 per violation per week [S2, S3]. The bill's covered-packer definition itself reflects how concentrated cattle buying has become [S3]. The bill died before any of this took effect.

Independent ranchers and feedlot operators would have gained a public library of real contract terms and guaranteed negotiated-market volume in their regions, improving the prices they can command. Because these are mostly family-scale businesses selling into a concentrated buyer market, their gain runs alongside better price competition in beef.

USDA's Livestock Mandatory Price Reporting program would have absorbed new duties — running the contract library, 14-day slaughter schedules, expedited carcass weights, and annual cutout yield data — with open-ended appropriations [S3]. More public data, more agency workload.
